title: Lessons from My Industrial Placement Year
excerpt: A year as a .NET Developer at Cantarus taught me more about software engineering than any lecture could. Here's what I took away.
content:
Finishing a year-long industrial placement is a strange feeling. You walk in knowing how to write code, and you walk out knowing how to build software — two very different things.

At Cantarus, I worked primarily in C# and JavaScript, integrating content management systems for clients across different industries. The work was real: deadlines that mattered, bugs that affected actual users, and code reviews from developers who had seen every mistake you could possibly make.

What I learned

Code is communication. The most valuable feedback I received wasn't about logic errors — it was about clarity. Well-named variables, small functions, and honest comments make code reviewable by your future self and your teammates. I rewrote a lot of functions that technically worked but were impossible to reason about.

Asking questions is a skill. I spent too long in the first month trying to solve problems independently before reaching out. Good engineers ask specific, well-researched questions early. That saves everyone time.

Systems matter more than language. The choice of C# or JavaScript mattered far less than understanding how the pieces fit together — how a CMS renders content, how an API call travels through the network, how a deployment pipeline catches errors before production.

What I'd tell my past self

Read the pull request descriptions. They contain the reasoning that the code itself cannot. And invest time understanding the business domain — knowing why a feature is being built makes you a much better judge of how to build it.

title: Getting Started with Playwright for Test Automation
excerpt: Playwright has quickly become my go-to tool for end-to-end testing. Here's how I got up to speed and what makes it stand out.
content:
Before my role at Ligentia, I had written unit tests but very little end-to-end automation. Playwright changed that quickly.

Playwright is Microsoft's testing framework for web applications. It supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, and has first-class bindings for JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and C#. We used the C# binding, which integrates naturally with the .NET ecosystem we were already using.

Why Playwright over Selenium?

Selenium has been the industry standard for years, but Playwright addresses several of its pain points. Auto-waiting is the biggest one — Playwright waits for elements to be ready before interacting with them, which eliminates most of the flaky tests caused by race conditions. It also has a much better developer experience: the trace viewer, video recording on failure, and the codegen tool for recording interactions are all genuinely useful.

Writing your first test

The structure is straightforward. You navigate to a page, interact with elements by role or text content, and assert on the result. Using semantic locators (like finding a button by its accessible name rather than a CSS selector) makes tests more resilient to UI changes.

The Page Object Model pattern works especially well with Playwright — encapsulating page interactions in reusable classes keeps tests readable and reduces duplication as your suite grows.

What to watch out for

Test isolation is important. Each test should set up and tear down its own state rather than relying on a particular execution order. Shared state between tests causes subtle, hard-to-debug failures. Start strict about this from day one.

title: Building My First Full-Stack App: What I Got Wrong
excerpt: My B2B e-commerce project taught me hard lessons about architecture, scope, and the gap between 'working' and 'maintainable'.
content:
The B2B e-commerce project I built in my first year was the largest thing I had attempted solo — a full web application with user authentication, inventory management, and a checkout flow. It worked. It was also a mess.

Looking back at that codebase with a year of professional experience is humbling. Here's what I'd do differently.

Structure first, code second

I started writing routes before I had a clear picture of the data model. The result was a schema that grew organically, accumulating inconsistencies that became harder to fix with each new feature. Spending a day drawing out the entities and their relationships before writing a single line of code would have saved me a week of refactoring.

The scope trap

Every interesting idea felt like it belonged in the first version. An admin dashboard, analytics charts, email notifications — each one individually reasonable, collectively disastrous for focus. The features that shipped were half-finished versions of things that should have waited for v2.

Ship a smaller thing completely rather than a larger thing partially. Users can't use half-finished features, but they can always ask for more.

What I got right

Using a REST API from the start, even though the frontend was simple, paid off. When I later added more complex client-side behaviour, the separation between data and presentation was already there. It's easier to keep concerns separated than to separate them later.

Also: version control from day one. Commit often, write meaningful messages, and use branches even when working alone. The habit is worth building before you're working on a team.
